questions.title: What is an object in JavaScript?
questions.answer: An object is a collection of keyed properties. Objects are non-primitive values, and variables can hold references to the same object.
questions.underTheHood: Objects have an internal [[Prototype]] link used during inherited property lookup. Property values may be primitives, objects, or functions.
pitfalls: const prevents reassignment, not property mutation.

questions.title: What are the different ways to create objects?
questions.answer: Objects can be created using literals, Object.create(), constructor functions, classes, and factory functions.
questions.underTheHood: Object literals usually inherit from Object.prototype. Object.create() allows explicit prototype selection. Constructors and classes create objects through new.
followUps: What is the difference between a factory function and a constructor?

questions.title: What is the difference between dot notation and bracket notation?
questions.answer: Dot notation accesses properties using identifier-like names. Bracket notation evaluates an expression to determine the property key and supports dynamic keys.
questions.underTheHood: Both access mechanisms use JavaScript property lookup. If a property is not found directly, lookup can continue through the prototype chain.
pitfalls: user.key accesses the literal property named key.
followUps: How do computed property names work?

questions.title: How do you add, update and delete object properties?
questions.answer: Assign a value to create or update a writable property. Use the delete operator to remove a configurable own property.
questions.underTheHood: Property operations follow property descriptor rules. An inherited property may be shadowed by a newly created own property.
pitfalls: delete does not remove non-configurable properties.
Deleting an inherited property from a child does not remove it from the prototype.

questions.title: How do Object.keys(), Object.values() and Object.entries() differ?
questions.answer: Object.keys() returns enumerable own string keys. Object.values() returns their values. Object.entries() returns key-value pairs.
questions.underTheHood: These methods enumerate an object's own enumerable string-keyed properties, excluding symbol keys.

questions.title: How does JavaScript compare objects?
questions.answer: Objects are compared by identity rather than structural equality. Two distinct objects are unequal even when their properties contain identical values.
questions.underTheHood: Strict equality checks whether both operands refer to the same object.
pitfalls: Identical object structures do not imply equality.
JSON.stringify() is not a reliable general-purpose deep equality solution.
followUps: How would you implement deep equality?
